blocks.en: To synchronize the germination of Arabidopsis thaliana seedlings and isolate the phenotypic effects of the stressor from baseline developmental variations, we did 4 days of stratification at 4 °C, which ensures homogeneous growth of the plants. Seed stratification suppresses the master dormancy gene DELAY OF GERMINATION 1 (DOG1) and its downstream regulators. This overcomes the genetic brakes holding back germination, shifting the hormonal balance from abscisic acid (ABA) to gibberellins (GA) and causing the enzymatic weakening of the seed coat, which allows the radicle to emerge [12].

blocks.en: Targeting salinity stress, which is the toxic ion accumulation in the root zones, we took inspiration from Liu et al. (2020) for the early pretest experiment settings. Col-0 Arabidopsis Thaliana seeds were grown on divided agar plates containing MS medium with either 0 or 100 mM NaCl. Seeds were surface-sterilized with 75% ethanol following 95% ethanol, stratified for 2 days at 4 °C in the dark, and grown at 22 °C under 16h light/8h dark cycle. Salt was built into the medium, so seeds germinated under a fixed 100 mM stress from the start, with no gradual ramp. This set up provided the foundational agar system experimental conditions, yet we continuously revise and optimize the methods. Furthermore, this set up was limited to the early phase 1 experiment on trehalose protectant, following phase 2 and 3, we adjusted experimental conditions depending on the application method and different protectants such as ACCD, AtLEA14, or Bopep4.

blocks.en: Targeting heat stress, we took inspiration from Auverlot et al. [3] for prolonged thermo-priming assays protocol designing. Initially, seeds are germinated and grown on Murashige and Skoog (MS) agar plates at 22 °C. Once the seedlings are 10 days old, they’re held at 37 °C for 5 days to induce acquired thermotolerance prior to subsequent higher stress damage, and then returned to 22 °C for 5 days of recovery. Following recovery, seedling survival and physiological damage are assessed and analyzed via quantitative readouts: fresh weight and chlorophyll content. Both the agar and soil based thermo priming assays are established based on this foundational framework and methodology, with specific parameters refined to accommodate our experimental setups.

blocks.en: At the beginning of the plant trials, we established the experimental protocol and assessed the initial response of the plants to NaCl and to different trehalose concentrations: trehalose at 0, 0.125, 0.5 and 1 mM, and NaCl at 0, 50, 100, 150 and 250 mM. We later observed severe bleaching of the leaves under 250 mM NaCl within 3 days of observation, and 150 mM also led to visible chlorosis; plants in both groups died quickly under osmotic stress. We also noticed that trehalose at both 0.5 and 1 mM suppressed plant growth. This is supported by research: feeding low amounts of trehalose blocks, or feedback-inhibits, the plant’s endogenous trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatases (TPPs). This triggers hyper-accumulation of trehalose-6-phosphate (T6P), which signals a false sugar abundance, disrupts starch allocation and induces developmental arrest [22]. At higher concentrations, the plant significantly upregulates trehalase, the enzyme that breaks trehalose down into glucose. This detoxifies the excess trehalose and prevents the toxic accumulation of T6P, and the released glucose acts as a metabolizable carbon source that rescues the plant from growth arrest. Concurrently, the intact fraction functions as an osmoprotectant, mitigating salt stress. Going forward, we set our plant experiments at 75 and 100 mM NaCl, with trehalose at 0, 5 and 10 mM.

blocks.en: From experimental set 7 onwards, we tested protectant effectiveness by application timing. Each experimental set includes a control, a pre-treatment, a co-treatment and a post-treatment group; the pre-treatment and post-treatment groups receive the protectant one day before and one day after the heat or salinity stress, respectively. With this application schedule we can test whether a protectant has to be applied before the stress surge, which is the role of our bioreactor, and whether a stress forecast from an AIoT prediction model and field stress sensors is needed.

blocks.en: On Day 0, sterilized Arabidopsis seeds were stratified on ½ MS neutral vertical agar plates for 4 days at 4 °C, and moved to the growth chamber for 4 days of germination. blocks.en: We did not use heat shock, as it is rarely observed in actual field conditions. Instead, thermo-priming for 3 days was used to simulate a slow change of temperature. Vertical plates cannot retain as much liquid protectant on the surface as horizontal plates can, so we used a spray nozzle that dispensed 0.536 mL for every 3 sprays. blocks.en: Abiotic stress, such as salinity stress and heat stress, negatively affects crop productivity. To test the effectiveness of our self-produced protectants under both types of stress, we chose to use a hydroponic system that allows for precise control of environmental factors. Compared with soil-based systems, hydroponics reduces the number of uncontrolled variables, such as differences in soil composition, microbial communities, and water distribution. Therefore, we can establish and maintain consistent experimental conditions by precisely controlling environmental parameters, including pH, electrical conductivity, temperature, and dissolved oxygen. In addition, nutrients and stress treatments can be delivered more uniformly to all plants through the nutrient solution, improving experimental consistency. Because treatments are added directly to the root environment, the hydroponic cultivation system allows us to rapidly observe plant responses to different stress conditions and evaluate the protective effects of our target protectants.

blocks.en: We are inspired by Matthew Gilliham’s hydroponics culture system (Conn et al., 2013) [5]. First, Arabidopsis seeds were sown on 0.6% agar containing black microcentrifuge-tube lids, each with a 3 mm diameter hole punched using a leather punch. Then, the lids containing seeds were placed on a microcentrifuge tube rack with the agar side facing down. Each well was filled with 2.1 mL of ½ MS medium, allowing the agar to remain in contact with the medium throughout stratification and germination. The seeds were stratified at 4 °C in the dark for at least 48 hours, and then transferred to a growth chamber maintained at 22 °C under a 16-hour light/8-hour dark photoperiod. After germination, 4-day-old seedlings were directly transferred onto the floating board or holder and left to grow in the hydroponic box. The tank was kept dark to reduce algal growth and continuously aerated with air stones to maintain sufficient dissolved oxygen. The nutrient solution was regularly replaced every 2–3 days, and the plants were then used for experimental treatments and physiological measurements.

blocks.en: To evaluate whether our protectants could reduce abiotic stress in plants, we developed multiple experimental platforms, not only agar systems. We needed a platform in which stress could be easily applied for different durations and the concentration of protectants could be precisely controlled. As a result, we can measure the fresh weight or root length of these treated plants, providing simple and accessible ways to quantify the results. In the beginning, we reviewed related papers to figure out how they established stress protocols on Arabidopsis. Here we focused on heat and salinity stress.

blocks.en: First, we followed Cortés-Jiménez et al. [8]. This experiment tested six NaCl concentrations, 0, 50, 100, 150, 200 and 250 mM, rescued by Azospirillum brasilense, the most studied plant growth promoting bacteria (PGPB). According to the results, plant stems under 0–100 mM NaCl did better than under 150–250 mM, and best at 50 and 100 mM NaCl. This means that these two salinity concentrations are moderate enough for the plant to be rescued by the bacteria. According to the pretests from agar, Arabidopsis applied with 100 mM NaCl expresses a strong stress response but doesn’t die at this threshold and could be rescued. Therefore, we decided to test 100 mM NaCl in our salinity test. Next, we decided to use CH Bio peptide to evaluate the stress response of plants under 100 mM NaCl. We used CH Bio peptide since it is a commercial product that helps plants resist abiotic stress.

blocks.en: One of our main reference papers on heat stress is Lee et al. [2], which describes how different stages of a plant may have different heat tolerance. This helped us make a quick decision about which developmental stage is most suitable for each condition, as well as the growth medium composition, the timing of stress application, and the days of recovery. This information was particularly important for us because this was our first time cultivating Arabidopsis on the hydroponic platform and our first heat treatment. We therefore designed the system around three variables: plant developmental stage → timing of protectant application → timing and intensity of stress. Integrating all of this information helped us accelerate our experiments and increase the success of protectant testing in the hydroponic system.

blocks.en: Soil trials were done to simulate real field conditions and allow protectants to be validated under complex conditions after testing in controlled environments such as agar and hydroponics. Soil introduces physical matrix interactions, including water retention and pore size distribution, which affect how the NaCl and protectant diffuse and reach the plant roots. Additionally, soil contains native microbial flora, allowing us to validate its real world viability. Hydroponics and agar assays are for baseline fine tuning, protocol simulations, and controlled proof of concept, while demonstrating efficacy in real soil reflects smallholder farming realities.

blocks.en: After determining the planting protocol, we optimized the plant growth stage by aligning our experiment timeline with the life cycle of Arabidopsis thaliana, because choosing the correct developmental stage is vital for capturing active metabolic and phenotypic responses. Arabidopsis progresses through a rapid life cycle of approximately 6 to 8 weeks, structured into distinct principal growth stages [1]: germination and seedling establishment (stages 0.1–0.7, days 0–7), when the radicle emerges through the seed coat, the cotyledons expand and the first true leaf appears; the rosette growth phase (stages 1.0–1.12, weeks 2–4), with exponential leaf expansion and primary root elongation; the floral transition and bolting (stages 5.0–6.5, weeks 4–5), driven by floral regulators such as LEAFY (LFY) and APETALA1 (AP1); and reproductive senescence (stages 8.0–9.0, weeks 6–8 and later), when resources are reallocated, chlorophyll breaks down and the siliques mature.

blocks.en: We initially conducted salinity assays on 1-month-old plants, at the late rosette to early bolting phase. At this developmental junction, Arabidopsis shifts its resource allocation toward floral meristem development rather than general vegetative homeostasis [15], and the lower leaves begin early senescence, which introduces baseline physiological variability into our assay data. The difference between stressed and unstressed plants may therefore be less obvious, which affects our conclusions on protectant efficacy. Following suggestions from Prof. Cheng, we moved our testing window to 2-week-old plants (stages 1.02–1.04). At 14 days after germination, Arabidopsis is in an active vegetative growth phase, and the absence of floral transition and senescence gives uniform tissue and reproducible experimental responses.

Following suggestions from Prof. Cheng, we moved our testing window to 2-week-old plants (stages 1.02–1.04). At 14 days after germination, Arabidopsis is in an active vegetative growth phase, and the absence of floral transition and senescence gives uniform tissue and reproducible experimental responses.

blocks.en: Salt behaves differently in soil than on agar, so the salinity concentrations and protectant doses had to be re-evaluated to maximize the observable differences in rescue effectiveness. Evaluating the protective efficacy of ACC deaminase requires a soil salinity model that induces measurable stress without causing immediate, lethal tissue necrosis. We evaluated two established soil salinization protocols on 2-week-old Arabidopsis thaliana in growth chambers: a top-down wash method [7], with direct surface application of 100, 200 and 300 mM NaCl until it washes through, and a sub-irrigation accumulation method [6], with successive doses of 100 mM NaCl in the bottom trays, drawn upward into the root zone by capillary action. In earlier trials, a gradual ramp of 25 mM NaCl per day up to 100 mM, adapted from Dr. Verslues’ suggestions, produced minimal phenotypic damage and did not separate the control from the ACC deaminase groups. As Prof. Cheng noted, sub-irrigation accumulation was also insufficiently stressful, because plain-water irrigation every 2 days flushed the accumulated ions out of the active root zone.

blocks.en: To resolve these problems, we developed a sequential top-drenching protocol for evaluating the three protectant timings (pre-treatment, co-treatment and post-treatment). Plants receive equal volumes (30 to 50 mL per pot) of 100, then 200, and finally 300 mM NaCl, with no freshwater irrigation in between to prevent salt leaching. Runoff at the base of each pot confirms that the root system is fully saturated, and each tray reservoir is kept 1 to 2 cm deep, holding 200 to 400 mL, so that the root zone stays in equilibrium with the salt solution. Instead of following a fixed calendar, the protocol repeats 300 mM NaCl until clear phenotypic markers appear.

blocks.en: To evaluate the thermal protective capacity of ACC deaminase, we adapted established thermo-priming frameworks to our soil platform, building on the heat stress assays of Auverlot et al. [3] and following the same method as our agar system. In the agar trials, 10-day-old seedlings were exposed to 37 °C for 5 days to induce acquired thermotolerance and sustained heat stress, followed by 5 days of recovery at 22 °C before survival, fresh weight, chlorophyll retention and anthocyanin accumulation were measured. Translating this framework to soil required adapting both the incubation parameters and the treatment schedule: two-week-old plants were placed in a 37 °C incubator for 5 days of heat stress, followed by 5 days of recovery in a 22 to 25 °C growth chamber.

blocks.en: Pre-treatment simulates applying bio-inoculants or seed coatings before an anticipated stress, for instance when a farmer sees a heatwave in the seasonal forecast. It allows beneficial bacteria to colonize the rhizosphere and prime the plant’s defenses before cellular damage occurs.

blocks.en: Co-treatment simulates application at the moment a stressor arrives, such as sudden soil salinization after flooding or fertilizer runoff. blocks.en: 100 mM NaCl suppressed plant growth severely, producing visibly stunted roots and reduced leaf blades across the 100 mM NaCl row of the plates (e–h). Among these salt-stressed groups, the roots of every trehalose-supplemented group bent towards the left, whereas the untreated stressed control grew straight down gravitropically (e). The roots are bending away from the saline environment, a behavior known as halotropism, or salt-avoidance tropism. Halotropism is driven mainly by the redistribution of the plant hormone auxin in the root tip, which lets seedlings reduce their exposure to salt by growing around it, and Arabidopsis has been shown to display this response under a salt gradient [23].

blocks.en: Three readouts support the rescue at 1.0 mM. First, in panel c the plants supplemented with 1.0 mM trehalose retained more chlorophyll under 100 mM NaCl than the untreated salt-stressed control, so the exogenous trehalose let them tolerate the salinity and limited the degradation of the photosystem. Second, primary root length in panel d shows the same pattern: the 1.0 mM group had the longest average primary root, 46.4 mm against approximately 35.8 mm in the untreated salt-stressed control. blocks.en: Contrary to our initial hypothesis, 5 mM trehalose did not have a protective effect under mild salt stress (75 mM NaCl) relative to the untreated stressed control; instead, the trehalose-treated group had reduced chlorophyll content (panel b). We had expected 5 mM trehalose to work better at the lower stress level, but it was effective only under 100 mM NaCl. This suggests that 75 mM NaCl is a mild salt stress, at which the plants’ endogenous regulatory systems can still maintain homeostasis without exogenous protectants. In contrast, 100 mM NaCl likely exceeds the plants’ tolerance threshold, triggering protective mechanisms that make more effective use of exogenous trehalose to mitigate cellular damage, so the 100 mM NaCl groups treated with 5 mM trehalose sustained significantly better growth than their untreated control.

blocks.en: The BoPEP4 co-treated plates (b, e, h) show progressive salt damage as the NaCl concentration rises from 0 to 100 mM. At 100 mM the damage is extensive chlorosis, with yellow-to-green leaf margins and partial leaf bleaching. Every co-treated plate also shows a green-to-yellow gradient from leaf to leaf, with round, spatulate leaves. Chlorosis across all the co-treatment groups suggests that BoPEP4 applied at the same moment as the stress is inhibitory in itself. At 75 mM the co-treated plate contains seedlings of varying sizes, mostly green rosettes with many chlorotic leaves, some whitish patches near the edges and little browning. At 100 mM (h) the phenotype is the most severe: chlorosis, whitish stems and hypocotyl bases, bleaching and early necrosis on some leaves. Even without salt, the co-treated plates grew less well than the unstressed mock control. The readouts agree: both the fresh weight and the relative total chlorophyll content of the unstressed co-treatment group fall below the mock-untreated control (panel c), and the chlorophyll falls much further.

blocks.en: Prolonged heat stress was applied by keeping seedlings at 37 °C in an incubator for 5 days, to simulate the prolonged rising temperatures of global warming. The phenotypes show consistent damage: severely stunted primary root elongation, a much smaller rosette area, and severe chlorosis with white and yellow bleached leaves compared with the mock-untreated control. This response matches the protocol of Auverlot et al. [3] and confirms that the stress treatment was effective.

blocks.en: Under 37 °C thermo-priming, ACC deaminase supplied at different timings gave different phenotypes. All heat-stressed groups given ACC deaminase had visibly longer roots, with pre- and post-treatment showing longer roots and better chlorophyll retention than the heat-stressed control, whereas co-treatment showed reduced survival and severe chlorosis. Co-treatment was also the least effective timing in the ACC deaminase salinity assay (experimental set 9). Across both salinity and heat stress, ACC deaminase was therefore more effective when applied before or after the stress than together with it.

blocks.en: This trial also shows that the application timing of ACC deaminase makes a significant difference to its effectiveness. Under 37 °C heat stress, adding ACC deaminase after the stress and the recovery period kept the most chlorophyll, followed by co-treatment and then pre-treatment. Ethylene production increases at two points, when heat is applied and when it is removed: after leaving the 37 °C incubator, plants enter recovery and produce ethylene to manage cellular damage and adjust their metabolism [18], [19].

blocks.en: To evaluate the salt sensitivity of Arabidopsis, 13-day-old Arabidopsis were treated with 100 mM NaCl for 7 days. CH Bio peptide treatments were performed using three different regimens, pre-treatment, co-treatment and post-treatment, in separate hydroponic boxes. The control group was also treated with 100 mM NaCl, but not treated with CH Bio peptide. In this test, the co-treatment group grew the best after salinity treatment. We found out that 100 mM of NaCl would cause significant stress on Arabidopsis but won’t cause death, which helped us to determine the appropriate NaCl concentration for further experiments.

blocks.en: Arabidopsis treated with B. subtilis WB800 cultures showed signs of stress under both pH conditions. At the 1 and 1/2 dilution factors the stress was most severe: leaves turned yellow and the plants were small. The 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 groups showed significant anthocyanin accumulation, a stress response visible as the darker color of the leaves. Based on these results, we decided to dilute the culture at least 16-fold in subsequent experiments.

blocks.en: We directly compared the sub-irrigation accumulation method [6] with the top-down wash (drench) method [7] on 2-week-old Arabidopsis thaliana. Seeds were stratified in 1 mL of sterile water for 4 days and dispersed evenly into soil pots with a micropipette, followed by selection for uniform rosette development. The accumulation method applied sequential sub-irrigation doses of 100 mM NaCl by tray capillary action, with plain-water irrigation between doses. The wash method applied sequential surface drenches of 100, 200 and 300 mM NaCl (30 to 50 mL per pot) without plain water until the pots were fully saturated and the root zone had equilibrated. Phenotype, fresh weight and chlorophyll were measured at the end of the stress cycle.

blocks.en: The sub-irrigation accumulation method did not induce sufficient osmotic stress, giving lush rosettes and a high average fresh weight of approximately 0.42 g, because the plain water between doses flushed accumulated ions out of the active root zone. In contrast, Prof. Cheng’s top-down drench gave a fresh weight of 0.15 g, a reduction of approximately 64%, which shows that top-down drenching impairs cell expansion and tissue water accumulation. The drench protocol produced clear, reproducible growth inhibition and salt stress symptoms without immediate lethal necrosis, which makes it the better method for high-concentration soil screening despite the lower baseline biomass. Both protocols gave comparable volumetric chlorophyll concentrations near 1.0 mg/L: under the milder accumulation method, pigment density stays high because chloroplast development is uninhibited, while under the wash method the smaller rosettes concentrate the remaining pigment.

blocks.en: The choice of salinity treatment is particularly important for evaluating protection by ACC deaminase. Under salinity stress, plants accumulate 1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylic acid (ACC), the precursor of the plant hormone ethylene. Although ethylene has important roles in normal development and stress responses, excessive stress-induced ethylene can inhibit root elongation and plant growth. Orozco-Mosqueda et al. [21] reviewed evidence that plant-growth-promoting bacteria with ACC deaminase degrade ACC into ammonia and α-ketobutyrate, reducing excess ethylene and helping plants maintain growth under saline conditions, which supports using biomass and growth traits to study ACC deaminase. A salinity treatment that causes little growth inhibition makes it hard to distinguish a protective effect from normal growth, while one that causes extensive tissue damage leaves too little viable growth to measure a rescue. The lower mean fresh weight under the top-down drench therefore makes it a promising method for ACC deaminase screening, provided the plants remain viable and the response is reproducible across biological replicates.

blocks.en: Under our conditions, 100 mM NaCl was not enough to induce clear visible stress, whereas symptoms became apparent at 300 mM, so 300 mM became our soil stress baseline. Because post-treatment was applied one day after the first 300 mM NaCl exposure, it can be seen as a delayed co-treatment given once salinity stress had developed, while the co-treatment groups were dosed while the stress was still mild. The detectability of a protective effect therefore depends on the severity of the stress: under insufficient stress, protected and unprotected plants are hard to tell apart, and under severe stress the tissue damage may exceed the protection the treatment provides.

blocks.en: The control pots show a healthy, centered rosette with dark green leaves and vigorous growth. Under 37 °C heat stress, the plants without ACC deaminase show clear wilting, reduced rosette size, leaf bleaching and lower overall biomass in both trials. Plants pre-treated with ACC deaminase before the heat show moderate leaf survival, although chlorosis and stunted leaf expansion are still visible in both trials. The co-treatment pots keep a fuller canopy, greener leaves and better structural integrity than the heat-stressed control, which points to some protection during sustained thermal stress. Post-treatment recovered unevenly: some green tissue is preserved, but most leaves show anthocyanin build-up (purple hues) and bleaching along the rims, and this group bolted the most and carried the tallest bolting stems of any group, so it was the most stressed under the conditions we set.

blocks.en: Post-treatment did least for plants under 37 °C heat, and in both trials its chlorophyll and its fresh weight came in below the heat-stressed control, which is what applying a protectant after the stress has already damaged the plant looks like. Pre-treatment held the most chlorophyll of the three timings in both trials, and exceeded the heat-stressed control in trial 1 though not in trial 2. On this platform the protectant therefore did most when it was already in place before the heat arrived, which is the argument for forecasting the stress and not waiting to react to it. The agar heat sets do not rank the timings the same way, so the two platforms do not yet agree on a best timing.

blocks.en: Our original approach was to build a dose-response curve from protectant concentration and a rescue index. The only runs with a repeat were ACC deaminase heat stress on agar and ACC deaminase heat stress in soil, and each of those has two trials, not three. We will aim for at least three independent replicates per condition, so that an improvement in fresh weight or chlorophyll content can be shown to be reproducible and not just read off a single plate or pot.

blocks.en: Replication is also what the timing comparison needs. We applied protectants at pre-treatment, co-treatment and post-treatment on agar and in soil, but the timing that performed best was not consistent across experiments. More replicates are what would settle which timing actually rescues the plants.

The preliminary comparison of sub-irrigation against top-down application produced limited visible growth inhibition under the watering conditions we tested, while the top-down application of 100, then 200, then 300 mM NaCl produced much clearer salinity symptoms.

blocks.en: Even so, the top-down method does not establish the salt concentration actually present around the roots. Drainage, dilution, evaporation and salt accumulation all change how much NaCl a plant takes up from the same applied dose. The next step is a standardized salinity schedule, with the three ACC deaminase timings compared against it, so that every pot receives the same salt load and the timings can be compared on equal terms. Once we have a treatment window, we will test intermediate times within it to find whether the effectiveness of ACC deaminase depends on a particular stage of stress development.

Future experiments should prioritize independent replicates, a more consistent treatment protocol, appropriate controls, and a dose-response series for ACC deaminase. attrs.en: The hydroponic box workflow drawn as one sheet. Down the left, preparation: box and board, seed holders, seed-holder agar, medium, and planting Arabidopsis seeds in the holders. Phase 1, NaCl with CH Bio peptide: 4-day-old seedlings into 300 millilitres of 0.1 times MS medium, 10 days old, then 600 microlitres of CH Bio peptide and 290 millilitres of medium with 10 millilitres of 3 molar NaCl, the peptide removed 3 days after, 7 days of observation. Below, the heat stress test: boxes into a 37 degree incubator, protectants added once the medium reaches 37 degrees, three days of observation, then the protectant removed, the plants moved to fresh medium and a 22 degree incubator for 7 days of observation.

Each labelled rack takes 2.1 millilitres of its master mix and 0.07 millilitres of 3 molar NaCl, the plants go back to the rack, and 7 days of observation follow.
